The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.

bivy.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
bivy.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers
bivy.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
bivy.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. Sources disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.notes: Everything in this file starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp in this file helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak in this file — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. bivy.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
bivy.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
bivy.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.

Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
bivy.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.notes: Everything in this file starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp in this file helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak in this file — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
bivy.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
bivy.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.

Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.

bivy.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
bivy.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow
bivy.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
bivy.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak in this file — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.

bivy.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season
bivy.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.

bivy.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
bivy.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group
bivy.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
bivy.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.

bivy.name: Entiat Meadows
bivy.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.
bivy.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. For this file it serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.

bivy.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
bivy.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy
bivy.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site in the file — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. bivy.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.

The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
bivy.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.
bivy.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE MOST RESTRICTED CAMP IN THE ZONE AND THE RULES ARE THE POINT. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp ONLY on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
bivy.notes: The base for MOUNT DANIEL and the eastern option for MOUNT HINMAN, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. THE CRITICAL 2026 CAVEAT: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.

bivy.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
bivy.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.
bivy.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
bivy.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For MOUNT DANIEL it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
bivy.capacity: Around forty sites at Klipchuck; the smaller campgrounds up and down the highway corridor add a few dozen more between them
bivy.water: Piped water at Klipchuck when the season's system is turned on, and Early Winters Creek nearby. Do not count on the tap outside the main season or in a drought year — check before you drive out, because the alternative is hauling water from town.
bivy.permit: Nightly campground fee. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for the trailhead lots. No wilderness permit required. Campfires are prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions currently in force, including in established rings, and the county burn ban applies as well. Some highway-corridor sites are closed in rotation for paving work between early August and mid September.
bivy.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one in this file with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near enough to walk to if you wanted. Coming from the west over the pass, this is the first campground on the dry side and the change is abrupt: open pine, no undergrowth, hot afternoons and cold clear nights. Use it as staging, not as a destination. The practical value is that it lets you drive out the evening before, sleep at the trailhead, and start the long Wolf Creek or Cedar Creek walk at dawn rather than in the heat of the day, which on these approaches matters more than it sounds. Bear in mind the highway itself opened late in 2026 after repair work, and paving through this corridor has been closing individual sites for stretches of a week or so at a time; ring ahead rather than arriving on spec.

bivy.name: Gardner Meadows, Wolf Creek trail
bivy.capacity: Numerous comfortable sites through the meadows and in the trees at their edge; this is the one place in the zone that will absorb several parties without crowding
bivy.water: A small stream flows south out of Gardner Mountain through the meadows and there is water at camp through a normal summer. This is the critical fill point: the Wolf Creek trail below is notably short of water for a valley-bottom trail, and everything above the meadows is bone dry. Carry the whole day's supply for the climb, and in a heat wave carry water up the approach as well — parties have turned around on these peaks for want of it.
bivy.permit: The upper Wolf Creek trail enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No wilderness permit or quota to hike or camp; sign the trailhead register. Party size limited to twelve people and eighteen head of stock. Northwest Forest Pass at the Wolf Creek trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions, and in a burned valley with standing snags this is a rule worth taking seriously. Proper food storage required.
bivy.notes: This is the basecamp for both peaks and the way the great majority of parties climb them. The Wolf Creek trail runs roughly ten miles up the valley bottom from the trailhead near Winthrop to meadows sitting directly beneath Gardner Mountain, with North Gardner a mile further northwest along the connecting ridge. From here a fit party can take both summits in a single long day and walk out the next morning. Know what the approach is now: the first eight miles or so run through forest burned in the 2021 fire, so there is very little shade, the tread is crossed by blowdown in places, and the second half is brushy. Where the trail turns uphill into the meadows it becomes genuinely hard to follow, buried in downed logs and regrowth, and one of the creek crossings is easy to miss even in daylight — this is not a route to be finding for the first time in the dark. Allow four and a half to five hours to camp with a climbing load. Season is July through September; the aspect is dry and eastern so the snow leaves early, but the same thing that clears the snow makes the walk in punishing in midsummer heat. The climbing above is a scramble on loose scree with pinnacles and short cliff bands on the connecting ridge that force you off the crest rather than along it.

bivy.name: High basin camp above Gardner Meadows
bivy.capacity: A small soggy basin with room for one or two tents; a party of two or three at most
bivy.water: A seep and small stream in the basin, which is what makes the site usable at all — it is boggy underfoot in early season and can be dry by late August in a poor snow year. Confirm it before carrying up on the strength of it, because there is no second option at this elevation and the retreat is all the way back to the meadows.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota, party limit of twelve, food stored properly. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions apply and there is nothing worth burning up here in any case. Camp on durable ground and off the wet meadow.
bivy.notes: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.

bivy.name: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
bivy.capacity: Good established sites for hikers and stock where the trail enters the meadows; several parties can spread out
bivy.water: Cedar Creek runs alongside for the whole approach and through the meadows, and it is the most dependable water in this file — a snow-fed creek in a north-facing valley that holds well into autumn. Fill here, because the climb east out of the valley toward the Gardner ridge has nothing.
bivy.permit: The Cedar Creek trail is outside the wilderness until it nears Abernathy Pass, where it enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota either side of that line; party limit of twelve inside. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Campfires prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions and the county burn ban.
bivy.notes: The western approach camp, and the reason to use this side at all. Cedar Falls comes at about 1.7 miles from the trailhead and is the day-hike turnaround for most visitors; keep going and roughly two miles beyond the falls the trail opens into meadows with good camping. From here the head of the valley and the west flank of North Gardner are within reach, and this is materially shorter than coming round by Wolf Creek. Its real value is seasonal. The trailhead is low and this is one of the first trails in the area to melt out, so in a late spring when Wolf Creek is still buried and the Gardner Meadows approach is a slog, this side goes. The trade is snow higher up and a steeper, less travelled finish. Damage from the 2021 fire is visible in this drainage too, heavier away from the creek than beside it, and the lower trail to the falls is in good order. The trail continues to Abernathy Pass at about 9.2 miles and over into North Creek, which is a useful escape or through-route if weather closes the tops.

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek head basin
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small parties; no established sites and no flat obvious platform
bivy.water: Snowmelt and the headwaters of Cedar Creek. Reliable in early season, which is when this camp makes sense; in late summer it thins out and the meadows below the falls become the better choice. Melting snow is the normal answer here in spring.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness at the head of the valley. No permit, no quota, party limit of twelve, proper food storage. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions, and there is no fuel. Leave no trace on unestablished ground and camp on rock or snow rather than fragile meadow.
bivy.notes: A spring and early-summer bivouac rather than a camp, used by parties taking the west side of North Gardner when snow still covers the ground. Getting into the head of the valley involves leaving the maintained trail and working up through brush, and it is not pleasant in dry conditions — the argument for it is precisely that on snow the brush is buried and the travel is fast. From the basin the west and southwest flanks of North Gardner rise directly, and a party can take both Gardner summits and be back at the car the following morning, which is appreciably shorter than the Wolf Creek round trip. Expect avalanche terrain on those slopes into June and treat the timing accordingly: an early start, firm snow, and off the slopes before the afternoon. There is no shelter, the basin is a cold sink, and there is no easy retreat except the way you came. This is a competent-party option in a narrow window, not a general-purpose camp.
