If the ground you intend to use is not an established site, say so when you book and expect to be routed to a cross-country zone permit arranged by telephone rather than online.
bivy.notes: A high, exposed alternative to the lake basin for a party that wants to be moving early on WHITE MOUNTAIN or that is traversing rather than going in and back. The pass sits at roughly 4,900 ft on the long shelf that carries the trail in a slow horseshoe between the Duckabush head and the East Fork Quinault, and Chimney Peak and the Anderson massif are both in view from it — which is the honest reason most people stop here rather than any advantage on climbing day. The trade is bad: it saves very little on either summit and it costs you shelter, water and any chance of a comfortable night. There is nothing to hide behind and the weather arrives off the Quinault with no warning. Treat it as a tactical stop on a longer route rather than a base. Snow lies on the north side of the shelf into midsummer and the meadow ground either side of the trail is soft enough to hold a footprint for years, so stay on rock or bare tread.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows and Camp Siberia — the West Fork Dosewallips side of LaCrosse Pass
bivy.capacity: Honeymoon Meadows is an open riverside meadow camp with several sites and is the pleasant one; Camp Siberia near Anderson Pass is smaller, higher and colder, with a few spots and an old shelter frame. Diamond Meadow and Big Timber lower down break the walk further.
bivy.water: Reliable at all of them — the West Fork Dosewallips runs beside the trail the whole way and the meadows carry side streams into the autumn
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The Dosewallips side is not a quota area and these camps are usually available at short notice, which is a real advantage over the Quinault approach to the same country. Animal-resistant food container required. Honeymoon Meadows sits near the fire line and Camp Siberia above it, so assume no fires at either.
bivy.notes: This is the eastern way to LaCrosse Basin and the one to use when the East Fork Quinault quota is gone. From the road end the trail runs up to Dose Forks at about 7.6 miles, Big Timber at 10.3, Diamond Meadow at 12.7 and Honeymoon Meadows at 15, with the LaCrosse Pass trail branching a little before that and Camp Siberia at around 16 near Anderson Pass. From Honeymoon Meadows the pass trail climbs roughly 2,000 ft in a couple of miles, the first 1,500 in forest before it breaks into open meadow, and drops the other side toward the LaCrosse Basin lakes — so MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN are two days in from here rather than one. THE ROAD IS THE CATCH AND IT HAS BEEN FOR TWO DECADES. The Dosewallips road washed out well below the old trailhead and has never been rebuilt, so the walk starts with several miles of abandoned road before any trail begins, and every mileage quoted above is measured from the old road end rather than from where you will actually park. Bicycles help on that stretch. Add the road walk to every figure before deciding this is the short way.

bivy.name: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
bivy.capacity: Four established sites on the river flat, and it is rarely contested — almost everyone walking this valley is bound for Low Divide and passes straight through
bivy.water: Reliable. The North Fork Quinault runs at the camp, which is also the reason the camp exists and the reason it can be unreachable; treat everything.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The North Fork Quinault is not a quota area, so this is one of the easier permits in the park, but nothing here is held back as a same-day walk-up and camps this far in do not always surface in an online search — telephone the wilderness information centre if it will not show. An approved animal-resistant food container is mandatory throughout the park wilderness and free loaners are handed out with permits. This camp sits below the 3,500 ft fire line, so fires are legal in the established rings when no seasonal ban is running, and bans are usual by midsummer.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for MOUNT LAWSON and effectively the only one. The peak rises about 3,800 ft above the river in a mile and a third, straight out of the drainage the camp sits in, and the climb is a class 2 slog on steep forest and open slope rather than anything technical — the work is the approach, not the summit. The camp is roughly twelve miles up the valley from the North Fork trailhead, past Wolf Bar, Halfway House, Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter, and the walk is gentle until the last few miles where the valley narrows and the trail climbs and drops across steep sidehill. THE FORDS ARE THE WHOLE PLANNING PROBLEM. There are three of them — Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and the North Fork itself right at this camp — and the river crossing here is regularly impassable during snowmelt or after heavy rain. Parties have been turned around at it having walked twelve miles. Go in late summer when the river is low, carry poles, and treat a high river as a trip-ending condition rather than something to force. Reach the trailhead by the North Shore Road; the South Shore Road has been washed out and a phone will still try to send you that way.

bivy.name: Elip Creek and the lower North Fork Quinault camps
bivy.capacity: Elip Creek has four sites, Wolf Bar five and Halfway House two. Trapper Shelter above them holds two small spots and is best treated as day or emergency use only rather than a planned night.
bivy.water: Reliable at all of them — the river or the named side creek. The lower valley is rainforest and water is never the constraint here.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance; not a quota area and usually obtainable at short notice. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. All of these sit well below the fire line so established rings are legal outside a burn ban.
bivy.notes: These break the walk to Sixteen Mile rather than serving any summit directly, and that matters more than it sounds: the drive to the North Fork trailhead is long, most parties arrive in the afternoon, and twelve miles with a climbing pack on the same day is an unpleasant way to start. Wolf Bar at about two and a half miles is the late-arrival camp, Elip Creek at roughly six and a half is the natural halfway stop, and Trapper Shelter a mile and a half further is the last of them before the valley steepens. Grades are easy to Trapper and then the trail begins working up and down high above the river. Two of the three fords are below Sixteen Mile, so a night here also lets you look at the water level before committing to the upper valley. Deep old-growth forest, heavy shade, mosquitoes in early summer and no views whatsoever — this is shelter and mileage, nothing more.

bivy.name: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail
bivy.capacity: A modest forested riverside camp with a handful of sites, quieter than the valley above it because most parties push the extra four miles to the chalet meadow
bivy.water: Reliable — the East Fork Quinault and the creek the camp is named for both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and THE EAST FORK QUINAULT IS A QUOTA AREA. It has been run under a nightly cap of thirty permits or roughly two hundred people since 2024, so this is a booking to make the day reservations open rather than a fortnight out. The summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and releases in one drop in mid-April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over plus a six dollar booking fee, or an annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY REQUIRED IN THIS VALLEY and enforced rather than advised — the Enchanted Valley was closed over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Free loaners at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness offices.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for CHIMNEY PEAK, and the reason it rather than the chalet meadow is that the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about nine miles, which is where this camp sits. Push on to the chalet and you have walked four miles past your own turning and given yourself them back again in the morning. The peak stands immediately north above the valley with its southeast face rising something like 4,800 ft in less than a mile, streaming waterfalls into the valley below — spectacular from the trail and completely useless as a line of ascent. The climb goes round to the southwest ridge and is class 3 scrambling once you are on it, with the first ascent not made until 1941, which says something about how the ground below it behaves. Expect a long, steep, largely trackless day out of the valley floor. June through September is the workable window. The walk in from Graves Creek is thirteen miles to the chalet with staged camps at Pony Bridge and O'Neil Creek before this one, so most parties take two easy days in rather than one hard one.

bivy.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.
bivy.water: Reliable — both lakes hold through the season and the outlet creeks run into autumn. This is the last dependable water before anything you climb from here; the slopes and the unnamed glacier between the two summits carry no running source once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
bivy.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. THE APPROACH IS THE ENTIRE DIFFICULTY AND THERE ARE THREE OF THEM, none short. From the Dosewallips you go up the West Fork and over LaCrosse Pass. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.

bivy.name: O'Neil Pass and the upper Duckabush shelf
bivy.capacity: Informal rather than developed — a small amount of workable ground on the shelf near the pass, room for a party or two, with no facilities of any kind
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal runnels only, and the pass itself dries out as the summer goes on. Fill at Lake LaCrosse or down in the basin before coming up; this is ground you carry water to.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. Which booking you need depends on the approach — the Duckabush side is not a quota area, the East Fork Quinault is. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. No fires at this elevation. If the ground you intend to use is not an established site, say so when you book and expect to be routed to a cross-country zone permit arranged by telephone rather than online.
bivy.notes: A high, exposed alternative to the lake basin for a party that wants to be moving early on WHITE MOUNTAIN or that is traversing rather than going in and back. The pass sits at roughly 4,900 ft on the long shelf that carries the trail in a slow horseshoe between the Duckabush head and the East Fork Quinault, and Chimney Peak and the Anderson massif are both in view from it — which is the honest reason most people stop here rather than any advantage on climbing day. The trade is bad: it saves very little on either summit and it costs you shelter, water and any chance of a comfortable night. There is nothing to hide behind and the weather arrives off the Quinault with no warning. Treat it as a tactical stop on a longer route rather than a base. Snow lies on the north side of the shelf into midsummer and the meadow ground either side of the trail is soft enough to hold a footprint for years, so stay on rock or bare tread.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows and Camp Siberia — the West Fork Dosewallips side of LaCrosse Pass
bivy.capacity: Honeymoon Meadows is an open riverside meadow camp with several sites and is the pleasant one; Camp Siberia near Anderson Pass is smaller, higher and colder, with a few spots and an old shelter frame. Diamond Meadow and Big Timber lower down break the walk further.
bivy.water: Reliable at all of them — the West Fork Dosewallips runs beside the trail the whole way and the meadows carry side streams into the autumn
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The Dosewallips side is not a quota area and these camps are usually available at short notice, which is a real advantage over the Quinault approach to the same country. Animal-resistant food container required. Honeymoon Meadows sits near the fire line and Camp Siberia above it, so assume no fires at either.
bivy.notes: This is the eastern way to LaCrosse Basin and the one to use when the East Fork Quinault quota is gone. From the road end the trail runs up to Dose Forks at about 7.6 miles, Big Timber at 10.3, Diamond Meadow at 12.7 and Honeymoon Meadows at 15, with the LaCrosse Pass trail branching a little before that and Camp Siberia at around 16 near Anderson Pass. From Honeymoon Meadows the pass trail climbs roughly 2,000 ft in a couple of miles, the first 1,500 in forest before it breaks into open meadow, and drops the other side toward the LaCrosse Basin lakes — so MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN are two days in from here rather than one. THE ROAD IS THE CATCH AND IT HAS BEEN FOR TWO DECADES. The Dosewallips road washed out well below the old trailhead and has never been rebuilt, so the walk starts with several miles of abandoned road before any trail begins, and every mileage quoted above is measured from the old road end rather than from where you will actually park. Bicycles help on that stretch. Add the road walk to every figure before deciding this is the short way.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. Sources differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is GLACIER camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.

bivy.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
bivy.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
bivy.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.

bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
